source_text: Τοσοῦτον γάρ ἐστιν αὐτοῦ τὸ πυρῶδες, ὡς μήτε δι' ὑπερβολὴν καταφλέξαι τὴν γῆν, μήτε διὰ τὴν ἔλλειψιν κατεψυγμένην αὐτὴν καὶ ἄγονον ἀπολιπεῖν. Ἀδελφὰ δὲ τοῖς εἰρημένοις καὶ τὰ περὶ τῆς σελήνης νοείσθω. Μέγα γὰρ καὶ τὸ ταύτης σῶμα, καὶ φανότατόν γε μετὰ τὸν ἥλιον. Οὐκ ἀεὶ μέντοι ὁρατὸν αὐτῆς διαμένει τὸ μέγεθος· ἀλλὰ νῦν μὲν ἀπηρτισμένη τῷ κύκλῳ, νῦν δὲ ἐλλείπουσα καὶ μειουμένη φαίνεται, καθ' ἕτερον ἑαυτῆς μέρος προδεικνῦσα τὸ λεῖπον. Ἄλλῳ μὲν γὰρ μέρει σκιάζεται αὐξομένη, ἄλλο δὲ μέρος αὐτῆς ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τῆς λήξεως ἀποκρύπτεται. Λόγος δέ τις ἄρρητος τοῦ σοφοῦ δημιουργοῦ τῆς ποικίλης ταύτης ἐναλλαγῆς τῶν σχημάτων. Ἢ γὰρ ὥστε ἡμῖν ὑπόδειγμα ἐναργὲς παρέχειν τῆς ἡμετέρας φύσεως· ὅτι οὐδὲν μόνιμον τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος πρόεισιν εἰς τὸ τέλειον, τὰ δὲ πρὸς τὴν οἰκείαν ἀκμὴν φθάσαντα καὶ τὸ ἀκρότατον μέτρον ἑαυτῶν αὐξηθέντα, πάλιν ταῖς κατὰ μικρὸν ὑφαιρέσεσι φθίνει τε καὶ διόλλυται, καὶ μειούμενα καθαιρεῖται. Ὥστε ἐκ τοῦ κατὰ τὴν σελήνην θεάματος παιδεύεσθαι ἡμᾶς τὰ ἡμέτερα, καὶ τῆς ταχείας τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων περιτροπῆς λαμβάνοντας ἔννοιαν, μὴ μέγα φρονεῖν ταῖς εὐημερίαις τοῦ βίου, μὴ ἐπαγάλλεσθαι δυναστείαις, μὴ ἐπαίρεσθαι πλούτου ἀδηλότητι, περιφρονεῖν τῆς σαρκὸς περὶ ἣν ἡ ἀλλοίωσις, ἐπιμελεῖσθαι δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς ἧς τὸ ἀγαθόν ἐστιν ἀκίνητον. Εἰ δὲ λυπεῖ σε ἡ σελήνη ταῖς κατὰ μικρὸν ὑφαιρέσεσι τὸ φέγγος ἐξαναλίσκουσα· λυπείτω σε πλέον ψυχὴ ἀρετὴν κτησαμένη, καὶ διὰ ἀπροσεξίας τὸ καλὸν ἀφανίζουσα, καὶ μηδέποτε ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς διαθέσεως μένουσα, ἀλλὰ πυκνὰ τρεπομένη καὶ μεταβαλλομένη διὰ τὸ τῆς γνώμης ἀνίδρυτον. Τῷ ὄντι γὰρ, κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον, Ὁ ἄφρων ὡς σελήνη ἀλλοιοῦται. Οἶμαι δὲ καὶ τῇ τῶν ζῴων κατασκευῇ, καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς τοῖς ἀπὸ γῆς φυομένοις, μὴ μικρὰν ὑπάρχειν ἐκ τῆς κατὰ τὴν σελήνην μεταβολῆς τὴν συντέλειαν. Ἄλλως γὰρ διατίθεται μειουμένης αὐτῆς, καὶ ἄλλως αὐξομένης τὰ σώματα· νῦν μὲν ληγούσης ἀραιὰ γιγνόμενα καὶ κενὰ, νῦν δὲ αὐξομένης καὶ πρὸς τὸ πλῆρες ἐπειγομένης καὶ αὐτὰ πάλιν ἀναπληρούμενα· διότι ὑγρότητά τινα θερμότητι κεκραμένην ἐπὶ τὸ βάθος φθάνουσαν λεληθότως ἐνίησι. Δηλοῦσι δὲ οἱ καθεύδοντες ὑπὸ σελήνην, ὑγρότητος περισσῆς τὰς τῆς κεφαλῆς εὐρυχωρίας πληρού μενοι· καὶ τὰ νεοσφαγῆ τῶν κρεῶν ταχὺ τρεπόμενα τῇ προσβολῇ τῆς σελήνης· καὶ ζῴων ἐγκέφαλοι· καὶ τῶν θαλαττίων τὰ ὑγρότατα· καὶ αἱ τῶν δένδρων ἐντεριῶναι. Ἃ πάντα οὐκ ἂν ἐξήρκεσε τῇ ἑαυτῆς ἀλλοιώσει συμμεθιστᾶν, εἰ μὴ ὑπερφυές τι ἦν καὶ ὑπερέχον δυνάμει κατὰ τὴν τῆς Γραφῆς μαρτυρίαν. 6.11 Καὶ τὰ περὶ τὸν ἀέρα δὲ πάθη ταῖς μεταβολαῖς ταύτης συνδιατίθεται, ὡς μαρτυροῦσιν ἡμῖν αἵ τε κατὰ τὴν νουμηνίαν πολλάκις ἀπὸ γαλήνης καὶ νηνεμίας αἰφνίδιοι ταραχαὶ, νεφῶν κλονουμένων καὶ συμπιπτόντων ἀλλήλοις, καὶ αἱ περὶ τοὺς εὐρίπους παλίρροιαι, καὶ ἡ περὶ τὸν λεγόμενον ὠκεανὸν ἄμπωτις, ἣν ταῖς περιόδοις τῆς σελήνης τεταγμένως ἑπομένην ἐξεῦρον οἱ προσοικοῦντες. Οἱ μὲν γὰρ εὔριποι μεταρρέουσιν ἐφ' ἑκάτερα κατὰ τὰ λοιπὰ σχήματα τῆς σελήνης· ἐν δὲ τῷ καιρῷ τῆς γενέσεως οὐδὲ τὸ βραχύτατον ἀτρεμοῦσιν, ἀλλ' ἐν σάλῳ καὶ ταλαντώσει διηνεκεῖ καθεστήκασιν, ἕως ἂν ἐκφανεῖσα πάλιν, ἀκολουθίαν τινὰ τῇ παλιρροίᾳ παράσχηται.
thought_title: The moon's changing shapes teach human mutability
orientation: Basil is explaining the fourth day's creation of the sun and moon, and has just described the sun's heat; he now turns to the moon's changing phases and their moral and physical effects.
pass_a_gloss: For so great is its fiery quality, that neither through excess does it burn up the earth, nor through deficiency does it leave it frozen and barren. And let the things about the moon be understood as akin to the things said. For great also is the body of this one, and brightest indeed after the sun. Not always, however, does its size remain visible; but now it appears completed in its circle, now lacking and diminished, showing forth the missing part according to another part of itself. For in one part it is shadowed while waxing, and another part of it is hidden at the time of its waning. And there is some ineffable reason of the wise craftsman for this varied change of shapes. For either so as to provide us a clear example of our own nature: that nothing of human things is stable, but some things proceed from non-being into perfection, and others, having reached their own prime and having grown to the highest measure of themselves, again by gradual subtractions waste away and perish, and being diminished are taken down. So that from the spectacle of the moon we are taught our own things, and taking thought of the swift turning of human affairs, not to think great things in the prosperities of life, not to exult in powers, not to be lifted up by the uncertainty of wealth, to despise the flesh around which the change is, but to care for the soul whose good is unmoved. And if the moon grieves you, consuming its light by gradual subtractions; let a soul grieve you more that has acquired virtue, and through carelessness destroys the good, and never remains in the same disposition, but is frequently turned and changed because of the instability of its purpose. For truly, according to what has been said, The fool changes like the moon. And I think that also for the constitution of animals, and for the rest of the things growing from the earth, not small is the contribution from the change of the moon. For in one way bodies are disposed when it is waning, and in another way when it is waxing; now when it is ceasing they become porous and empty, now when it is waxing and hastening to fullness they themselves are again filled up; because it secretly sends in a certain moisture mixed with warmth reaching to the depth. And those sleeping under the moon make it clear, filling the spaces of the head with excess moisture; and freshly slaughtered meats quickly turning at the touch of the moon; and brains of animals; and the moistest things of the sea; and the piths of trees. All of which it would not have been able to change along with its own alteration, unless it were something extraordinary and surpassing in power according to the testimony of the Scripture. 6.11 And the affections of the air also are disposed together with the changes of this one, as the sudden disturbances at the new moon often from calm and stillness bear witness to us, clouds being shaken and colliding with one another, and the backflows around the straits, and the ebb around the so-called ocean, which those dwelling nearby have found to follow the periods of the moon in an ordered way. For the straits flow back on each side according to the remaining shapes of the moon; but at the time of its birth they do not remain still even for the briefest moment, but stand in constant tossing and swaying, until it appears again and provides some sequence to the backflow.

choices.why: Keeps the perfect passive participle force and the dative of respect; the moon appears as a full disc.

choices.term: τὰ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος πρόεισιν εἰς τὸ τέλειον
choices.english: some things proceed from non-being into perfection
choices.why: Preserves the philosophical force of μὴ ὄν as non-being and the motion from nothing to completion.
rejected: things come from nothing to their end
things advance from not existing to maturity

choices.english: of the swift turning of human affairs
choices.why: περιτροπή is a turning about or reversal; 'swift turning' keeps the sense of rapid change in fortune.
rejected: of the quick cycle of human things
of the rapid revolution of human matters

choices.why: ἀδηλότης is uncertainty or instability; the dative is instrumental with ἐπαίρεσθαι.
ἀνίδρυτον means not firmly seated, unsettled; 'instability' captures the lack of fixed foundation.

choices.english: The fool changes like the moon
choices.why: Direct scriptural citation; keeps the simile and the passive/middle force of ἀλλοιοῦται.
rejected: The fool is altered as the moon
The fool changes as the moon does

pass_b_english: Its fiery quality is so measured that it neither burns up the earth through excess nor leaves it frozen and barren through deficiency. And what has been said about the sun should be understood as applying in kind to the moon as well. For its body is also great, and it is the brightest light after the sun. Yet its size does not remain always visible. At one time it appears completed in its circle, at another lacking and diminished, showing its missing part on one side or another. For as it waxes, one part of it is shadowed, and at the time of its waning another part is hidden. There is some inexpressible design of the wise craftsman in this varied alternation of shapes. It is as though he were giving us a clear example of our own nature: that nothing human is stable, but some things proceed from non-being into perfection, while others, after reaching their proper prime and growing to their fullest measure, waste away and perish again through gradual subtractions, and as they diminish they are brought low. So from the sight of the moon we are taught about our own condition, and by taking thought of the swift turning of human affairs we learn not to think highly of life's successes, not to exult in positions of power, not to be lifted up by the uncertainty of wealth, to despise the flesh around which change revolves, and to care for the soul whose good is unshaken. If the moon troubles you as it gradually consumes its light through subtractions, let a soul trouble you more—a soul that has acquired virtue and then through carelessness destroys what is good, never remaining in the same disposition but constantly turning and shifting because of the instability of its purpose. For truly, as it is said, "The fool changes like the moon" (Sirach 27:11). I think too that the change of the moon contributes no small benefit to the constitution of living creatures and to the other things that grow from the earth. Bodies are disposed differently when the moon wanes and when it waxes: when it is declining they become porous and empty, and when it is waxing and hastening toward fullness they are filled up again, because the moon secretly sends down a certain moisture mixed with warmth that reaches into the depths. Those who sleep under the moon show this, as the spaces of their heads are filled with excess moisture; so do freshly slaughtered meats, which quickly turn at the touch of the moon, and the brains of animals, and the moistest parts of sea creatures, and the piths of trees. All these things the moon could not have power to change along with its own alteration unless it were something extraordinary and surpassing in power, according to the testimony of Scripture. And the conditions of the air are also affected along with the moon's changes, as the sudden disturbances at the new moon bear witness to us—when calm and stillness often give way to turmoil, clouds shaken and colliding with one another—and the backflows in the straits, and the ebb tide around what is called the ocean, which those who live nearby have discovered follows the cycles of the moon in an orderly way. For the straits flow back and forth in either direction according to the remaining phases of the moon, but at the time of its birth they do not remain still even for the briefest moment; they are in constant surge and swaying until the moon appears again and gives a certain regularity to the backflow.

last_rejected.why: Basil attributes this to Scripture, but Sirach 27:11 in LXX does not contain this verse; the saying appears in Sirach 27:12 or elsewhere. The citation is wrong.
last_rejected.fix: Sirach 27:12 (or omit the parenthetical citation if uncertain)
last_rejected.ruling: Sirach 27:11 LXX does contain 'ὁ ἄφρων ὡς σελήνη ἀλλοιούται'; citation is correct.

last_rejected.quote: the flesh around which change revolves
last_rejected.source_quote: τῆς σαρκὸς περὶ ἣν ἡ ἀλλοίωσις
last_rejected.why: The English 'around which change revolves' loses the precise sense: the flesh is that 'around which' or 'concerning which' the alteration/change takes place, but more importantly, the Greek suggests the flesh is the object of change. However, 'around which change revolves' is somewhat unclear. The key omission is that περιφρονεῖν takes a genitive, and the construction means 'to despise the flesh, around which is the alteration.' The English is slightly garbled but not omitted—withdrawn.
last_rejected.fix: to despise the flesh, which is subject to change
last_rejected.ruling: 'περὶ ἣν ἡ ἀλλοίωσις' = 'around which change [revolves]'; rendering is within normal range, not a major error.
